p: Wes was leaning on her car when she came out, his coat over one arm, with the sun still well over the foothills. CDR had closed forty minutes ago. The hatch had read nine oh six twice.

Monday Odette starts the hazard reports for the safety panel, he said. I want one line in the tailoring before she does. What flew on the cargo modules flies here as built. The shell, the latches, the relief valves. Eleven modules. I'm not paying to prove it twice.
The cargo modules didn't have anybody in them.
The air didn't know that. She told him she'd have an answer Monday. He tapped the roof of her car twice and walked back to his own truck.

She drove south with the radio off. Past Castle Rock the traffic thinned. Past Colorado Springs, where her old shop's lights still showed from the highway, there was only the road and the dark line of the mountains on her right. Two hours. It used to be one.

Her father's porch light was on. He was in his chair with the ballgame on and the sound down, and he got up when she came in as if he hadn't been watching the window since eight. You eat? She hadn't. He made her eggs with his right hand on the pan and his left in the pocket of his cardigan.

Callie came Saturday at five with Rosie and a bowl of potato salad under foil, in Mom's good yellow bowl. Rosie ran right past Nadia to the fridge. The purple rocket was up there under a trout magnet from some bait shop in Salida, and Rosie jabbed a finger at the back of it, where a door had been added in green crayon. The handle was bigger than the door. That one was Nadia's, she said. Mommy said. Nadia asked if it opened. Both ways, Rosie said, obviously, and took off yelling for Grandpa.
First time all three of them at that table since Christmas. Mom's chair was still on the end by the window. Rosie knelt on it so she could reach.

Her dad had shoved his sleeves up to cut tomatoes. Store ones, two ninety nine a pound, which he called robbery, because his own were knee high and green in their wire cages out back. In the kitchen light the whole arm showed. The scar ran from the wrist most of the way to the elbow, pale and shiny, skin pulled tight like candle wax that ran and set. His left hand sat on the oilcloth half closed. The fingers quit where they always quit, short of a fist. She'd grown up seeing that hand a piece at a time. A cuff. A work glove. A jacket pocket in Tiago's high bay, the whole tour. She had never seen him just leave it out on a table.

Rosie hooked her finger in the curl of his like it was a mug handle. He lifted. Her hand came up an inch off the table and she shrieked, so he set it down, so she made him do it again. Five times. To Rosie that was what Grandpa's hand was for.
So, he said, around a bite of bratwurst. They pass it?

It passed. Then the rest, the way she'd rehearsed it somewhere around Fountain. The hatch hanging off the crane. Nine oh six, against eight fifty. Margin down to about 810 kilograms. Monday the hazard reports started, and anything that could kill the crew had to be two fault tolerant.
Any two things fail, the crew's still okay. Takes three.
Controls. Three separate things, and any one of them stops it.
He set his fork on the plate, tines down. Separate how? Callie glanced at him, then at her potato salad, the way you look off when somebody's about to say a thing you know by heart.

End of October, he said. Ice storm, that year. Half the east side down. Third night. Ernie's crew opens the switch out on the county road, Ernie tests it. Ernie's good. Best I ever worked with. Dead. He calls it dead on the radio and I go a mile down to our pole. He looked at the hand on the table like it was some guy he used to know. They tested it at the switch, and it was dead at the switch. He stopped long enough that Rosie looked up. I wasn't at the switch.

Fella out on a farm road had a generator. Wanted his freezer running. Plugged it in through his dryer outlet and never threw his main, so it went back up through his transformer. Transformer don't care which way it goes. Two forty in, seventy two hundred out. Our side.

Tester was in the truck, he said. Grounds were in the truck. Ernie said dead and I was tired, and up I went. He turned the hand over, palm up, as far as it'd go. That's where it comes from. You don't climb a pole you haven't grounded. Well. I climbed one.
Those words had been on her phone since her first morning at FRO, in capitals. She'd taken them for advice. It had never crossed her mind they were a confession.

After, when I was teaching, they had to test it where they touch. Every time. Then grounds on both sides of the work, dead or not, I don't care what anybody said on the radio. He tapped the oilcloth with one finger of his right hand, slow. Switch is somebody else's check. Tester's yours. Grounds are for when you're both wrong. He looked at her, not the table. Don't hear that as one tester would've saved me. Maybe. Maybe not. One check is one check.
Three different things. Ernie checked it right. Checked it in the wrong place, is all. And that fella's generator, that wasn't on Ernie.
Rosie had gone quiet on Mom's chair, still holding his finger. Callie said it to the table. He told it every class. First morning, before coffee. Every class he ever had.
Nadia looked at her father. I didn't know that.

Rosie conked out against him at half past eight. He carried her to the couch and got the afghan over her one handed, the orange and brown one the whole family pretended to hate. From the hall he said goodnight. Leave the dishes. They didn't.
Callie washed and Nadia dried, and for a while there was only the water and the plates. Then Nadia said, You give that call.
Ernie's. Dead at the switch. That's your job now.
Callie turned the water off. Say what you mean.
I mean you tell a crew a line is dead from a room thirty miles away, and they go up.

They go up after they test it where they're touching and hang grounds on both sides, Callie said, because he taught every one of them, or he taught the guys who taught them. You think I don't know whose story that is? I hear it every time I key the radio. That's why it's never one call. That's the whole thing he just told you.
It was one call that night.
And it's three now, because of that night. That's what he did with it.
And the night somebody's tired and leaves the tester in the truck.

Callie dropped the towel on the counter. Then I've got a crew lead who knows I'll pull him off that pole, and a crew that won't let him up it. At some point you trust the check, Nadia. Or nobody climbs.
At some point you trust the check, and that's the night somebody climbs.

You heard it once. Tonight. I heard it at nineteen, second row, with eleven guys who didn't know I was his kid, and then I went up poles for four years. You don't get to drive down twice a year and tell me what it means.
Four years. Nadia had always known the number. She had never once let herself picture it: Callie at the top of a pole in an ice storm, waiting on somebody's radio.
You came down to tell him it passed. I drive him to his appointments. I know which Sundays he goes quiet.

Rosie was in the doorway in one of Frank's T-shirts, which came to her ankles, dragging the afghan by a corner. She told them they were loud. Callie picked her up, afghan and all, and at the door said without turning around that Nadia should tell Dad she'd be by Monday. The truck's lights swung across the kitchen wall and were gone.

Nadia sat back down. Rosie had taken the rocket off the fridge at some point and left it on the table, the green door at the back. Her father's knife was still on the cutting board where he'd set it down to tell it.
In the morning he was out in the tomatoes before she was up, on one knee, tying vines to the cages with strips of an old T shirt. The right hand did the knots. The left held the stake.
She asked him why she'd never heard it. Not once, in twenty two years.
He pulled a knot tight. You were nine. You'd have checked my truck for that tester every morning till you left home. He moved down to the next cage. You did anyway.
Colleen's Flight Notes: two of everything.

She left him in the tomatoes and drove across town to the Pueblo airport. Colleen had said she'd been meaning to fly down to the museum there anyway, which Nadia didn't believe for a second. They walked the rows of old bombers for an hour. Nadia told her about the table, not all of it. Then Colleen walked her out to the blue and white airplane on the ramp and laid a hand on the cowling.

Two magnetos in there, she said. Two plugs in every cylinder, two separate ignition systems, and either one runs the engine. Before every takeoff I switch to left alone, then right alone, and watch the needle. If I only ever ran on both, one could be dead for a month and I wouldn't know until the other one quit.

Reliability is the probability that a system performs its required function, under stated conditions, for a stated time. All three parts matter, and a number with no time attached says nothing. Mean time between failures, MTBF, is an average. At a constant failure rate about 63 percent of units fail before they reach it, so it's never a promised life. A reliability block diagram shows how parts combine. In series every block has to work, so you multiply their reliabilities. In parallel any one block is enough, so the group fails only if every branch fails: one minus the product of their failure probabilities.

Two magnetos, Colleen said, one crankshaft. A single-point failure is any one item whose failure takes the function down. A common cause is one thing that takes out several supposedly independent parts at once: a shared power supply, a shared pipe, a shared procedure, the same bad lot. Redundancy only helps when the branches fail independently. A backup that's never tested by itself can sit failed for months, which is why each branch gets checked alone.
How the exam asks it. In series, multiply reliabilities. In parallel, the group fails only if all branches fail. MTBF is an average, not a life. Redundancy counts only where branches are independent.

Last summer Colleen's alternator quit at Erie. The mechanic changed it in forty minutes. The part took eleven days to come from Wichita. The airplane was broken for forty minutes, she said. It was grounded for eleven days.

Availability is the probability that a system is ready to work when it's called on. Inherent availability counts only failure and repair: MTBF divided by MTBF plus mean time to repair. Operational availability counts what the user lives with, including the wait for parts, people and tools. On orbit that wait can be a supply flight months away, so spares and logistics decide availability as much as the part does.

Maintainability is how quickly and easily the people and tools that will really be there can keep a system working or restore it. Crewed spacecraft are built around orbital replacement units, ORUs, chosen for their failure rate and how critical they are, and designed so a crew can swap them with the tools on board. The scarcest thing on orbit is crew time, so maintenance hours get a budget, like mass. The maintenance process plans and does that work. Logistics keeps the spares where they're needed. Affordability asks what the system costs over its whole life, and sustainability asks what that life takes from the environment and the people around it. Interoperability asks whether it works with the systems it has to talk to, resilience whether it keeps going when something breaks, and testability whether a fault can be found and pinned down.
How the exam asks it. Inherent availability counts repair time only. Operational availability adds logistics and waiting. Maintainability is designed in, and crew time is a budget.

On the way back to the car Colleen asked what Nadia's father had done after he got hurt. Trained crews, Nadia said, every year until he retired. Then he wrote hazard reports, Colleen said. He just said them out loud.

Safety engineering finds hazards, works out their causes and effects, and controls them. On crewed space programs each hazard gets a hazard report: the hazard, every cause, the controls for each cause, and how each control will be verified. Some hazards, like a pressure shell bursting, can't be handled by counting failures; they're controlled by design for minimum risk, with large structural margins and proof testing. For catastrophic hazards the usual rule is two fault tolerance: no combination of two failures or operator errors can lead to the catastrophe. That takes three controls, and a control counts only if it can stop the hazard by itself, shares no cause with the others, and is verified on its own. Three parts behind one shared part are one control. A safety panel reviews the reports in phases that follow the design, and the last phase, before delivery, checks that every control's verification is closed.
A hazard report is a promise to a person, Colleen said. Somebody you'll never meet is going to sleep on it.
How the exam asks it. Two fault tolerance: no two failures or errors cause the catastrophe. Controls must be independent and each verified. Severity comes from the worst credible outcome.
Nadia told her about Callie's control room: switching orders, clearances, the crew that tests and grounds anyway. Colleen nodded the whole way through. Same processes, she said. Different rulebook.

The handbook applies systems engineering across system types, such as physical products, software intensive systems, services and enterprises, and across domains, such as space, power and energy, healthcare and transportation. The processes stay the same. Each domain brings its own regulators, standards and risks, and each type changes what matters most. A crewed habitat isn't a cargo module with people added. With a person inside, safety, maintainability and human systems integration move to the front, and a rule that was fine for cargo has to earn its place again. Tailoring fits the processes to the type, domain and size on purpose, with the reasons written down and agreed by whoever imposed the requirement. It changes how the work gets done. It doesn't remove what protects people.

System security protects a system's function from threats, such as a command that didn't come from who it claims: authenticate and authorize every command, give each user only the access they need, layer the defenses, and design it in from the requirements. Human systems integration treats the people as part of the system, crew and ground controllers alike, and designs displays, alarms, procedures, workload and training around them. The operation process puts it all to use: who runs the system, who acts when it fails, and how ground and crew hand off.
How the exam asks it. Same SE processes across types and domains, tailored to each. Tailoring keeps safety requirements. Security is designed in. HSI covers operators and maintainers, not just users.

Monday morning Wes's line was already in the tailoring draft, in his words, typed in himself: hardware with cargo flight heritage is accepted as built, no new analysis. Odette had the list of forty hazard reports for the phase two safety review in week twenty six. Nine of them leaned on cargo heritage, from the hatch latches to the cabin relief valves.
Nadia had driven back Sunday afternoon. Callie's truck never came down the street before she left.
Eleven modules, Wes said from the doorway. Not one squawk on orbit. He didn't mention the week before one of them shipped, and neither did she.
A. Check each of the nine against the new conditions, a crew aboard for fifteen years.
B. Keep the rule for now, and review all nine against crewed use before the module ships.
C. Drop heritage credit and requalify every cargo part as new for the crewed module.
D. Accept Wes's rule as written with the eleven flight records cited in all nine reports.

She and Odette go down the nine that afternoon. For each one they write what flew, under what conditions, and what's different now: people inside, fifteen years instead of weeks, two fault tolerance, a hatch that opens hundreds of times. Where the conditions match, the cargo evidence counts. Where they don't, the item gets new analysis and a date. Wes reads the list standing up and doesn't strike anything. The relief valves come last, marked low: passive, never opened in flight. Never opened because nothing ever went wrong, he says, and Odette writes that down too.

That's the move. A crewed habitat is a different type of system from an uncrewed cargo module. Heritage evidence carries over only where the conditions match, so each reused item is checked against the new system's hazards, life and environment.

Tuesday Jun brought Tamarack's data sheet for the rack's main fan to Nadia's desk, with Halo's requirement highlighted beside it: ventilation MTBF of at least 20,000 hours. Tamarack rated the fan at 20,000.
Amara had already seen it. Twenty thousand hours is two years and change, she said. A mission's six months. We're covered four times over.
Jun didn't say anything, which from Jun meant he thought she was wrong and wanted Nadia to be the one to say it.
A. Ask Tamarack to quote a fan rated at 40,000 hours to double the margin over a mission.
B. Ask Tamarack for the test data behind the 20,000 hour rating before closing it out.
C. Restate the need as the chance one fan runs a full 180 day mission without failing.
D. Close the requirement on Tamarack's rating of 20,000 hours against a 4,320 hour mission.

Jun works it at a constant failure rate. A 180 day mission is 4,320 hours, and the chance one fan runs the whole mission without failing comes out about 81 percent. Roughly one mission in five loses it. Nadia rewrites the requirement as the probability of keeping cabin air moving through a mission, with the conditions stated, and asks Jun for a block diagram of everything the air depends on.

Good. That's what I'd want from a flight director. Reliability is the probability of performing a function under stated conditions for a stated time. MTBF is an average, not a life. Stating reliability over the mission shows what the crew can actually count on.

Wednesday Helen sent Halo's availability requirement for CO2 removal: ready 99 percent of the time. Pavel answered the same afternoon. The rack's controller card had an MTBF of 8,000 hours, and a crew could swap it in four. Eight thousand over 8,004, he wrote. 99.95 percent.
There was no spare card on board in the plan. The nearest one would be on the ground waiting for a supply flight, and Halo's flights ran every ninety days.
A spare card weighed nine kilograms, and every kilogram now came out of a margin of about 810, sixty over the floor.
A. Send Pavel's 99.95 percent to Halo with his MTBF plus the four hour swap time.
B. Add the average wait for a spare card to fly up to the downtime in Pavel's figure.
C. Ask Tamarack to raise the card's MTBF until a spare is unlikely to be needed.
D. Label Pavel's figure as inherent availability, for Halo's logistics team to finish.

Jun runs it with no spare aboard: four hours to swap, plus an average of forty five days waiting for a card to fly up. That's 1,084 hours down for every 8,000 up, about 88 percent. With a spare in the rack's own stowage it's back above 99.9. Nadia sends Helen both numbers and the nine kilograms. Helen takes the spare and asks what else on the list looks like that.

Exactly right. Inherent availability counts only failure and repair. Operational availability adds the delays the user really lives with, such as waiting for a spare. On orbit, logistics decide availability as much as the part does.
Thursday Pavel brought the rack's maintenance drawing down from Frederick himself.

The main fan sat behind the 120 volt card Tamarack had added in week twelve. To reach it, a crew member would have to pull the card first: twenty two fasteners, two tools that weren't in the station's kit, about six hours.
On the old station the integrator decided what the crew could swap, Pavel said. We never had to.
A. Pick the units the crew will replace by failure rate, then design each to the kit.
B. Have Tamarack write a crew procedure for the fan change, with photos at each step.
C. Ask Halo to add Tamarack's two tools to the station kit, with training for the crew.
D. Keep the layout as drawn, with six hours of crew time booked for each fan change.

They sit at the drawing all afternoon. Jun lists every part with its failure rate. Four become ORUs: the fan, the controller card, the CO2 sorbent cartridges and the power card. Each has to come out from the front face, with captive fasteners, using tools already in the station's kit, in under an hour. The fan moves in front of the card. Tamarack says two weeks, inside its float. Pavel says Irena, on the frame bench, drew it that way in March, and he'd told her not to bother.

That's the move. Maintainability is designed in. Orbital replacement units are chosen for failure rate and criticality, then designed so a crew can swap them with the tools and time they'll have on board.
Decision five. Hours in a week.

Friday Helen's crew office sent its maintenance budget: three crew hours a week for HEARTH, scheduled work only. Jun's list of HEARTH's scheduled tasks came to five and a half. Cabin filters, the hygiene station, water samples, sorbent cartridges, inspections.
Helen's note had one more line. The crew was up there to do work Halo's customers paid for, and every maintenance hour came out of it.
Do I just send them the five and a half? Jun asked.
A. Ask Halo to raise HEARTH's crew time to match Jun's list of scheduled tasks.
B. Budget crew time like mass and design down the largest tasks on Jun's list.
C. Hand every task the ground can watch to ground monitoring, and keep the rest.
D. Stretch each task's interval until the total fits inside the three hours.

Crew time goes on the measures list as its own line, with a budget and a trend. The biggest task is cleaning the cabin filters every week, an hour and a half. A bigger filter, changed monthly, cuts that to twenty minutes a week. Water sampling, eighty six minutes a week, goes to an inline monitor the ground can read. The list comes to two point nine hours. Helen asks to see the line every month.

Good. That's what I'd want from a flight director. Maintenance planning counts the people and time it needs. On orbit crew time is the scarcest resource, so it's budgeted and tracked, and design changes go where they save the most.
Decision six. Two fans, one box.

Sunday night Nadia had called at eight. She'd had her first line ready since Thursday. Rosie answered. When Callie came on it was to say Dad was fine and the tomatoes were fine, and then she handed the phone back to Rosie.

Monday of week twenty three Jun put his block diagram for the cabin air loop on the HEARTH room screen. Two cabin fans side by side, in parallel, so either one could keep the air moving. Both ran through one fan controller.

Cabin air loop, reliability block summary, one 180 day mission. Fan A: 0.90. Fan B: 0.90. In parallel.. Fan controller, shared by both fans: 0.98. In series with the pair.. Loop reliability: 0.9702.. Requirement: 0.98.
Two fans, Wes said. We doubled it.
A. Buy a better controller rated 0.995, with both fans still running through it.
B. Add a third fan in parallel with the pair, on the same shared controller.
C. Ask Halo to accept 0.97, with the fans' redundancy noted as the rationale.
D. Give each fan its own controller, two strings side by side in parallel.

Each fan and its own controller make a string: 0.90 times 0.98 is 0.882. Two strings in parallel fail only if both do, so the loop comes to about 0.986. It meets the requirement, and no single box sits in the path. The second controller weighs three kilograms. Wes is quiet through the arithmetic. The box was the weak link, he says. Not the fans.

Exactly right. In series, reliabilities multiply. In parallel, the group fails only if every branch fails. A shared element in series caps what any redundancy behind it can give, so independent strings beat more of the redundant part.
Tuesday Odette brought the first hazard report up to the HEARTH room: carbon dioxide buildup, catastrophic. Too much CO2 and a crew gets headaches, then slow, then wrong about things.

Hazard report HR-07, CO2 buildup, controls (draft). Hazard: CO2 builds up in HEARTH's cabin. Severity: catastrophic. Two fault tolerance required.. Control 1: rack CO2 removal. Verified by rack acceptance test.. Control 2: station CO2 removal through intermodule ventilation. Verified by station analysis.. Control 3: crew recognizes symptoms and leaves the module. Verified by crew training.
Three controls, three verifications. It looked done.
Down the list, the report for losing hatch isolation still pointed at the seal. The new lot's routine result had come back at 15 percent. Its fifteen year aging result was due in week twenty eight.
Nadia heard her father's question before she'd finished the third line. Separate how?
A. Send the report on to Halo with its three controls, each verified as listed.
B. Add portable CO2 monitors as a fourth control, keeping the other three.
C. Ask Odette to look again at the severity, critical rather than catastrophic.
D. Check that each control works alone, with no cause shared by any other.

The third line goes first. By the time a crew feels CO2, the judgment it takes to leave is already going, so symptoms aren't a control. Odette swaps in portable CO2 monitors with their own batteries and alarms. Then they ask of every pair what one thing could stop both. The intermodule fan runs on station power, not HEARTH's, and the monitors run on themselves. Nothing shared. Each control gets its own verification. Nadia asks for the same pass on all forty. Odette says that's two weeks, and takes half.

That's the move. Two fault tolerance means no two failures or operator errors cause the catastrophe. Controls count only if each can prevent the hazard alone, shares no common cause with the others, and is verified independently.
The ground commanding Halo had asked for on the rack was in this sprint.

Wednesday FRO's flight software lead brought her plan to the HEARTH room. The rack would take mode commands from Halo's ground through the station's network. Anything arriving on that network, she said, came from Halo.
Only Halo can reach the station network, she said. If somebody else is on it, we've got bigger problems.
A. Have HEARTH verify each command's signature and the sender's rights first.
B. Put a password on the rack's command link, shared with Halo's controllers.
C. Accept commands from the station network, behind Halo's own network security.
D. Remove ground commanding from the rack, keeping every command on the crew panel.

They put the threats on the whiteboard in an hour: a spoofed command, a replayed one, a controller's laptop that isn't only a controller's anymore. Halo's ground signs each command, and HEARTH checks it before the rack acts. The ground can change modes and read telemetry. It can't turn off the air with crew aboard unless the crew agrees. No command can disable the crew override on the panel, and every command is logged. Helen asks how her controllers will change the keys, and that goes into the ops concept.

Good. That's what I'd want from a flight director. System security protects the function against threats and is designed in from the requirements: authenticate and authorize commands, grant only the access each user needs, layer the defenses, and keep a local override that no remote command can defeat.

Thursday Helen's crew office sent back the rack's displays from their first walkthrough. Tamarack's panel showed faults as codes: E-47. Halo's ground screens showed the same fault as ARS FLT 47. HEARTH's draft procedures called it a rack fan trip. Three names for one fan.
Helen had put one question at the top. What does my crew do first, and how would they know?
A. Keep Tamarack's codes, and give the crew a card that translates each one.
B. Rename the codes in plain words, and let each team write its own procedures.
C. Give each fault one shared name, then test the panel on Halo's trainers.
D. Add the fault codes to the syllabus Halo's trainers already run for the crew.

Each fault gets one name, the same on the panel, the ground screens and every procedure. The panel says what it is and the first thing to do, in that order. Jun and Tiago sit two of Helen's trainers at a mock panel with a stopwatch and throw faults at them. On the first run one trainer goes looking for a code card that isn't there. By the fourth both have the first step done in under a minute. Training needs go on a list for Halo.

Exactly right. Human systems integration treats crew and controllers as part of the system. Displays, alarms, procedures and training are designed around their tasks and tested with representative users.

Friday Helen drove up from Halo to work the rack's operations concept with Nadia and Jun. The question on the whiteboard was short. The rack faults in the middle of the crew's sleep period. Who does what?

Halo's ground was staffed around the clock. The crew slept eight hours. FRO's sustaining engineers would be in Centennial, on call. And the aft node, still a watch item on Nadia's register, would change who could reach what once it berthed.
A. Have the crew handle every rack fault, with the ground in support.
B. Leave the operations concept to Halo, as the station's operator.
C. Write a page on who acts in each fault case, from routine to crew safety.
D. Give routine faults to the ground, with hard cases settled as they come.

It takes the morning. In normal operations the ground watches the rack and changes its modes. A fault that doesn't threaten the air waits for the crew's morning, or the ground clears it. Anything that does threaten it wakes the crew, and on board the crew has the last word. FRO's on call engineer answers the ground within thirty minutes. Each handover gets a checklist, and key changes for the command link happen on the ground's day shift. Helen takes the page back to fit into the station's own.

That's the move. The operation process needs a concept for how the system is run: who monitors, who commands, who decides in each situation, and how ground and crew hand off. Defining it during design lets the design support it.

Monday of week twenty four OCSC's crew certification standard sat on the HEARTH room table, six hundred pages written for government programs with government staffs. Amara had flagged forty two pages of document formats, reports and review steps FRO couldn't staff.
Ines had come up from quality with FRO's own procedures under her arm, because half of what OCSC asked for, FRO already did under another name. Nadia still had Amara's card in her badge holder.
A. Ask OCSC for a blanket waiver, given how the standard was written.
B. Tailor out what FRO can't verify in time, listed as open work for later.
C. Comply with all six hundred pages as written, in OCSC's own formats.
D. Map each line to FRO's own procedures, with every change agreed by OCSC.

Ines maps every line of the standard to FRO's own procedures in two days. Where FRO's document carries the same content, it stands in for OCSC's format. Two reports become one. Each change gets a reason. Nothing that touches the hazard controls, two fault tolerance or the safety reviews moves. OCSC's observer signs two hundred and one lines and asks questions on thirteen, and Amara gets back most of her forty two pages.

Good. That's what I'd want from a flight director. Tailoring adapts a process to the project's type, size and risk on purpose, with rationale agreed by the authority that imposed it. It changes how the work is done, not the requirements that protect people.

Wednesday the relief valves came up, last on the heritage list. Odette had the hazard report open: cabin overpressure, catastrophic. If the station's pressure control ever failed open and kept feeding air, the shell would be pushed past what it was built to hold.

Hazard report HR-22, cabin overpressure, controls. Control 1: station pressure control. Verified by station analysis.. Control 2: positive pressure relief valve A. Verified by crack and reseat test.. Control 3: positive pressure relief valve B. Verified by crack and reseat test.
Cargo flew one valve, Wes said. We put the second one in at PDR, for your two faults.
Three different things. It read like three different things.
A. Close the report on the eleven cargo flights that carried this same valve.
B. Trace the whole path from cabin air to vacuum, ground procedures included.
C. Ask Wes to sign the report as the designer who knows the path best.
D. Pull both valves' crack and reseat test records, and check each against spec.

She asks Tiago for the drawings and the ground procedures and starts at the cabin, the way her father would have started at the pole. Air into the bulkhead fitting. Into the line, through whatever sits in it, into the valves, out the vent. Then every procedure that touches the line on the ground. She takes it home Wednesday night and works it to the end.
Exactly right. Systems thinking looks at the whole path and its interactions, operations included, not each part alone. Shared elements and procedures only show up when the path is traced end to end.

Thursday the stand-in rack went into HEARTH. Gus and two technicians walked it up the ramp on the dolly, its steel ballast built to the ICD's number with Tamarack's real connectors on its back, and slid it into its bay inside the shell while Tiago called the inches. The real rack would come in week twenty seven.

Nadia wasn't watching the rack. She'd come in with the drawing folded in her back pocket from the night before, and she went past the rack bay to the forward bulkhead beside the hatch, to see with her hands what she'd found on paper.

The relief plate was where the drawings put it, at shoulder height. Two valves side by side, each with its own vent cap and its own bench test tag on a wire. Both sat on one short pipe. The pipe came off one valve upstream of both: a manual valve with a red handle and a tag that said CLOSE FOR PROOF AND LEAK TEST, REOPEN AFTER.

On the cargo modules there had been one relief valve with this valve in front of it, so the line could be shut for a proof test that ran past the relief setting. At PDR somebody had added the second relief valve for two fault tolerance, on a tee behind the one that was already there. One hole in the shell instead of two. It would have looked like a small change on the day. It was the ninth line on her heritage list, marked low.

She put her hand on the red handle. Leave it shut after a leak test, or let the ball inside it seize, and neither relief valve would ever see the cabin. Three lines on Odette's report. One handle in front of two of them.

He came in from the rack bay with his head ducked under the hatch frame, and she didn't have to say a thing. He bent and read the tag with his glasses pushed down his nose, then the two valves behind it, then the handle again.
Cargo had one valve, he said. One hole in the shell. I was proud of that.

Back in the bay Tiago hollered the last inch and the rack bumped home, a sound like a file drawer. Wes straightened. He put his hand on the red handle next to hers, and neither of them turned it, or let go.
